items.abstract:
<jats:p><p>The change management field has operated with a binary diagnostic framework for six decades: willing versus resistant. Populations that fail to adopt evidence-based improvement methodologies are assessed for motivation and treated accordingly — with communication campaigns, incentive structures, champion networks, and leadership commitment protocols. This paper argues that this diagnostic framework fails for a specific and consequential class of innovations: those whose adoption requires a metacognitive register that the adopting population does not yet inhabit. Where this condition obtains, what presents as resistance is more precisely described as architectural imperception — the genuine inability to perceive the innovation rather than the unwillingness to adopt it. Standard change management interventions applied to this condition fail systematically because they address motivation in the presence of a perceptual development problem.</p>
<p>The paper names this condition the Perceptual Threshold Problem and develops its theoretical architecture across three moves. First, it traces the structural assumption Rogers' Innovation Diffusion Curve did not examine — that the population capable of perceiving an innovation is equivalent to the population exposed to it — and identifies the conditions under which that assumption fails. Second, it documents a regional natural experiment across five Alaska Native organizations spanning two decades — Mt. Edgecumbe High School, the Chugach School District, Chugachmiut, the Alaska Native Tribal Health Consortium, and Sealaska Corporation — that produces a pattern of success and failure consistent with the Perceptual Threshold Problem as the primary causal mechanism. Third, it proposes twelve falsifiable propositions that distinguish architectural imperception from attitudinal resistance and generate a prospective research agenda capable of confirming or disconfirming the theoretical claims.</p>
<p>The paper grounds its argument in W. Edwards Deming's foundational but undertheorized insight — that individual transformation is discontinuous, arriving as a threshold event rather than accumulating through training and incentive — and asks what the conditions are that make that discontinuity possible, what the guide must do to prepare the ground, and what genuine threshold crossing looks like when it arrives. It concludes by proposing the Shaman's Trail visual system — integrating the Russell affect circumflex, the dynamic body budget graph, and a sequential illustrated pedagogy in the tradition of Shook and Rother's Learning to See — as the structured first encounter with the relational field that makes threshold crossing possible in community healing contexts. The construct of Relational Tacit Knowledge is introduced to name the perceptual attunement the crossed threshold produces and that the apprenticeship architecture transmits.</p>
<p>The paper's implications extend across lean and organizational excellence practice, Indigenous health and governance implementation, and change management theory. Its central diagnostic contribution — the distinction between attitudinal resistance and architectural imperception — is offered as a prior category that the change management field requires before motivation-targeted interventions can be responsibly deployed.</p>
<p>&nbsp;</p></jats:p>
title: The Perceptual Threshold Problem: Why Rogers' Diffusion Curve Fails for Metacognitively Complex Innovations
